questions.question: What is the difference between an S3 bucket policy and IAM policy?
options: They are identical

S3 bucket policy: resource-based, attached to bucket, controls access from any principal including cross-account. IAM policy: identity-based, attached to user/role, controls access to multiple resources.
questions.explanation: Both can grant S3 access. S3 bucket policies: enable cross-account access without assuming a role, restrict access to specific VPCs or IPs, allow public access. IAM policies: user/role-level control. Combined: ALLOW on both = access.

questions.question: What is an Application Load Balancer (ALB) vs Network Load Balancer (NLB)?
options: ALB is faster
ALB: Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), URL path routing, host-based routing, WebSocket, Lambda targets. NLB: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), ultra-low latency, static IP, preserves source IP, handles millions of RPS.
questions.explanation: ALB: ideal for microservices, container-based, HTTP routing rules (path/host/headers), integrates with Cognito for auth. NLB: gaming, IoT, financial trading (sub-millisecond), supports TLS pass-through, Elastic IP.

questions.question: What is Auto Scaling predictive scaling?
options: Manually schedule capacity
Uses ML to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively scale capacity ahead of load — launches instances before demand hits, avoiding warm-up delays during traffic spikes.
questions.explanation: Predictive scaling (EC2 Auto Scaling): trains on 14 days of history, forecasts demand, launches instances before predicted load. Combine with dynamic scaling (reactive) for best results. Reduces scaling lag.

questions.question: What is AWS Direct Connect and when would you choose it over VPN?
options: Always choose VPN

Dedicated private physical connection from on-premises to AWS — provides consistent 1-100 Gbps bandwidth, lower latency, reduced data transfer costs. Choose over VPN for: large data volumes, latency-sensitive apps, compliance.
questions.explanation: Direct Connect: no internet, predictable performance, reduced bandwidth costs, dedicated port. VPN: encrypted, quick setup, internet-based, variable performance. Direct Connect + VPN: for encryption over Direct Connect.

questions.question: What is S3 Transfer Acceleration?
options: A CDN service
Speeds up S3 uploads by routing through CloudFront edge locations using AWS's global backbone network — most beneficial for large files uploaded from far-away geographic locations.
questions.explanation: S3 Transfer Acceleration: upload goes to nearest CloudFront PoP → travels AWS backbone → arrives at S3 bucket. Free to test at s3-accelerate-speedtest.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com. Cost: $0.04-$0.08 per GB.

questions.question: What are Amazon S3 storage classes and when to use Intelligent-Tiering?
options: Only S3 Standard exists

S3 Standard (frequent access), Standard-IA (infrequent, 30-day min), One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive, Intelligent-Tiering (unknown/changing access patterns — auto-moves between tiers).
questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering automatically monitors access and moves objects between frequent/infrequent access tiers. No retrieval fees. Small monitoring fee ($0.0025/1K objects). Ideal for unpredictable access patterns.

questions.question: What is Amazon SQS visibility timeout?
options: The time a message stays in the queue
After a consumer receives a message, it becomes invisible for the visibility timeout period. If not deleted before timeout, message reappears for another consumer. Default: 30s. Max: 12 hours.
questions.explanation: Visibility timeout prevents double-processing. Set it slightly longer than your max processing time. If processing fails, message reappears after timeout for retry. DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) handles messages failing after N retries.

questions.question: What is AWS Lambda cold start and how can you minimize it?
options: Lambda always starts instantly

Latency incurred when Lambda initializes a new execution environment for the first time or after idle period. Mitigation: Provisioned Concurrency (pre-warms), keep functions small, use efficient runtimes (Node.js/Python).
questions.explanation: Cold start: Lambda container init + runtime init + function init. Provisioned Concurrency pre-initializes environments (cost: $0.015/GB-hour). Use Lambda SnapStart (Java) for up to 10× faster startup. Python/Node have shorter cold starts than Java/.NET.

questions.question: What is Amazon Aurora Global Database?
options: Aurora across multiple AZs

A single Aurora database spanning multiple AWS regions — one primary region for reads/writes, up to 5 secondary read-only regions with <1 second replication lag. Enables disaster recovery with RPO<1s, RTO<1min.
questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database: primary region handles writes, replicates to secondaries via dedicated replication infrastructure (not database replication). Failover: promote secondary to primary in <1 minute. Ideal for global apps with low-latency reads.

questions.question: What is the difference between SQS Standard and FIFO queues?
options: Identical behavior
Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering. FIFO: 300 TPS (3000 with batching), exactly-once processing, strict order guaranteed within a message group.
questions.explanation: Standard: maximum throughput, possible duplicate messages (design for idempotency), approximate ordering. FIFO (First-In-First-Out): strict ordering, no duplicates, limited to 300 TPS per message group. Use FIFO for financial transactions.

questions.question: What is AWS Transit Gateway?
options: An internet gateway
A hub-and-spoke network transit hub that connects VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect gateways centrally — eliminates complex VPC peering mesh, supports multicast and route tables per attachment.
questions.explanation: TGW replaces complex VPC peering (N×(N-1)/2 peering connections). Attach: VPCs, VPNs, Direct Connect GWs, SD-WAN. Route tables control which attachments can communicate. Inter-region peering connects TGWs globally.

questions.question: What is AWS PrivateLink vs VPC Peering?
options: They are identical

VPC Peering: connect two VPCs for private traffic (no transitive routing). PrivateLink: expose a specific service endpoint privately via Interface Endpoint — traffic stays on AWS network, no VPC routing required.
questions.explanation: VPC Peering: VPC-to-VPC private connection, bidirectional. PrivateLink: expose a service (your NLB) or AWS service via private endpoint — consumers connect to endpoint, no VPC peering needed, scales to thousands of consumers.

questions.question: What is DynamoDB provisioned vs on-demand capacity?
options: Identical pricing

Provisioned: specify RCUs/WCUs, use Auto Scaling — cheaper for predictable workloads. On-demand: no capacity planning, scales automatically, more expensive per request — good for unpredictable or spiky traffic.
questions.explanation: Provisioned capacity with Auto Scaling: set min/max, DDB scales. On-demand: pay per request ($1.25/million WRU). Provisioned with steady workload: ~$0.65/million write. On-demand costs ~2× provisioned for steady traffic.

questions.question: What is AWS Elastic File System (EFS) vs FSx for Windows?
options: EFS works on Windows too

EFS: managed NFS (Linux only), POSIX-compliant, auto-scales. FSx for Windows File Server: managed SMB share, Windows ACLs, Active Directory integration — for Windows workloads needing shared file storage.
questions.explanation: EFS: Linux/Mac NFS v4.1, elastic scaling, IAM + POSIX permissions. FSx Windows: SMB/NTFS, Windows ACLs, Multi-AZ deployment, DFS Namespaces, Active Directory. FSx for Lustre: HPC/ML high-throughput workloads.

questions.question: What is AWS Cognito?
options: An authentication service for internal users only
Provides user pools (authentication — sign-up, login, MFA) and identity pools (authorization — temporary AWS credentials for authenticated users from social/corporate/Cognito providers).
questions.explanation: Cognito User Pools: managed user directory, supports MFA, social federation (Google, Facebook), SAML/OIDC. Identity Pools: exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentials (STS) to access AWS services directly from client.

questions.question: What is the AWS Well-Architected Framework Reliability pillar?
options: Only about backups

Ensures workloads perform their intended function correctly and consistently: automatic failure recovery, test failure scenarios (Chaos Engineering), horizontal scaling, capacity management, change management.
questions.explanation: Reliability design principles: automatic recovery from failure (CloudWatch alarms → Auto Scaling), test recovery procedures (AWS FIS - Fault Injection Simulator), scale horizontally (stateless architecture), stop guessing capacity.

questions.question: What is Route 53 latency-based routing vs geolocation routing?
options: They use the same logic

Latency-based: routes to the region with lowest latency from the user's location — based on actual network latency measurements. Geolocation: routes based on user's geographic location (country/continent/default).
questions.explanation: Latency routing: best performance (sends to lowest-latency region, which isn't always the geographically closest). Geolocation: compliance/localization (European users → EU endpoint). Geoproximity: shift traffic by bias values.

questions.question: What is AWS Config vs AWS CloudTrail?
options: They are the same

CloudTrail: records who made what API calls and when (audit trail of actions). AWS Config: records what AWS resources look like and tracks configuration changes over time (compliance/drift detection).
questions.explanation: CloudTrail: 'who did what' — API calls, console logins, resource creation. Config: 'what does it look like' — resource configuration snapshots, compliance rules (e.g., 'all S3 buckets must have server-side encryption'). Use both together.

questions.question: What is EBS gp3 vs gp2?
options: gp2 is newer

gp3: independently configure IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput (up to 1,000 MB/s) from storage capacity — more flexible, 20% cheaper than gp2 at same size. gp2: IOPS tied to size (3 IOPS/GB, burst to 3000).
questions.explanation: gp3: provision IOPS/throughput independently (3,000 IOPS/125 MB/s baseline free), then pay for additional. gp2: burstable IOPS based on size, unpredictable. Migration from gp2 to gp3: no downtime, instant type change.

questions.question: What is AWS DataSync?
options: A database migration service
An online data transfer service that automates moving large datasets between on-premises storage (NFS, SMB, S3-compatible) and AWS storage services — up to 10× faster than open-source tools.
questions.explanation: DataSync: agent-based (on-premises), encrypted transfers, bandwidth throttling, scheduling, validation. Use for: NFS/SMB to EFS/FSx migration, S3 migrations, data processing pipelines. Alternative to direct S3 sync for large datasets.

questions.question: What is Amazon EMR?
options: A managed relational database

Elastic MapReduce — a managed big data platform running Apache Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and Presto on EC2 instances. Process petabytes of data, scale cluster dynamically, use Spot Instances for cost savings.
questions.explanation: EMR provides managed open-source frameworks at scale. Master/Core/Task nodes. Transient clusters (launch, process, terminate) vs persistent. Integrates with S3 (EMRFS), DynamoDB. Cost: EC2 + EMR per-hour fee.

questions.question: What is Amazon EventBridge?
options: A network bridge service
A serverless event bus that connects AWS services, SaaS apps, and custom applications using events — routes events to targets (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions) based on rules and patterns.
questions.explanation: EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events): event-driven architecture. Default bus (AWS events), custom bus (your events), partner bus (SaaS events — Zendesk, Datadog). Archive, replay, schema registry included.

questions.question: What is CloudFront Origin Shield?
options: A WAF feature

An optional caching layer in CloudFront between edge locations and the origin — reduces origin load by collapsing cache misses from all edge locations into fewer requests to a single origin shield region.
questions.explanation: Without Origin Shield: each edge PoP independently fetches cache misses from origin. With Origin Shield: all cache misses route through one regional layer first. Reduces origin requests by up to 90% for global distributions.

questions.question: What is AWS Service Quotas?
options: A billing feature
A centralized service to view and manage limits (quotas) for AWS services — request quota increases, set CloudWatch alarms when approaching limits, track quota usage.
questions.explanation: AWS services have default quotas (e.g., 5 VPCs/region, 20 EC2/instance type/region). Service Quotas dashboard shows current limits, usage, and lets you request increases. Some quotas can be increased automatically.

questions.question: What is the difference between EC2 instance types T, M, C, R?
options: No difference

T: burstable performance (baseline CPU + credits for bursts) — dev/test. M: balanced compute/memory/storage — general-purpose production. C: compute-optimized (high CPU) — HPC/ML inference. R: memory-optimized — databases/caching.
questions.explanation: Instance families: T (burstable/dev), M (general production), C (CPU-heavy: ML training, batch), R (memory: Redis, in-memory DBs), X (extra memory: SAP HANA), P (GPU: ML training), I (storage: high IOPS NVMe).

questions.question: What is S3 Object Lock?
options: A server-side encryption feature

Prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a specified retention period — WORM (Write Once Read Many) compliance. Governance mode: privileged users can delete. Compliance mode: no one can delete during period.
questions.explanation: S3 Object Lock: immutable storage for compliance (SEC, FINRA, CFTC). Retention period: set per object or bucket default. Legal hold: preserves indefinitely until explicitly removed. Must enable at bucket creation.

questions.question: What is Amazon Macie and what does it do?
options: A threat detection service
A data security service using ML to automatically discover and protect sensitive data (PII, financial data, credentials) in S3 — identifies buckets with overly permissive settings.
questions.explanation: Macie scans S3 objects using pattern matching and ML. Findings: sensitive data types discovered, S3 bucket exposure (publicly accessible, lacks encryption, overly permissive ACLs). Integrates with Security Hub and EventBridge.

questions.question: What is an EC2 placement group?
options: A security group for EC2

Three strategies for placing EC2 instances: Cluster (same AZ rack, low latency/high bandwidth), Spread (different hardware, maximize HA, max 7/AZ), Partition (separate racks, HDFS/Kafka-scale isolation).
questions.explanation: Cluster placement: <10ms latency, up to 100 Gbps, for HPC/ML — risk: rack failure affects all. Spread: each instance on different hardware rack — HA for critical instances. Partition: large distributed systems, rack-level fault isolation.

questions.question: What is AWS Secrets Manager vs Systems Manager Parameter Store?
options: Identical services

Secrets Manager: automatic rotation (Lambda), cross-account access, native RDS/Redshift/DocumentDB rotation, higher cost. Parameter Store: hierarchical config, free tier available, no automatic rotation.
questions.explanation: Use Secrets Manager for: database credentials needing auto-rotation, compliance requirements. Parameter Store: application config, non-sensitive parameters (free Standard tier), sensitive strings (SecureString with KMS).

questions.question: What is an AWS Service Control Policy (SCP) limitation?
options: SCPs grant permissions directly

SCPs don't grant permissions — they only restrict what permissions can be granted. Even if an IAM policy grants full admin, an SCP restricting EC2 means EC2 actions are denied. Management account is exempt from SCPs.
questions.explanation: SCPs are guardrails, not grants. Effect: most restrictive policy wins (IAM Allow + SCP Deny = Deny). Management account bypasses SCPs. SCPs don't affect service-linked roles. Tested with IAM Access Analyzer.

questions.question: What is AWS Fargate Spot?
options: Regular Fargate with spot pricing
Fargate Spot runs ECS/EKS tasks on spare AWS capacity at up to 70% discount — tasks can be interrupted with 2-minute warning. Suitable for batch jobs, fault-tolerant workloads.
questions.explanation: Fargate Spot = EC2 Spot Instances but for serverless containers. Use with ECS capacity provider strategy: mix Fargate (stable) and Fargate Spot (cheap for non-critical tasks). Interrupted tasks get SIGTERM + 2 minutes to clean up.

questions.question: What is AWS Global Accelerator vs CloudFront?
options: They do the same thing

Global Accelerator: TCP/UDP traffic optimization using AWS backbone for any application (gaming, VoIP, APIs). CloudFront: HTTP/S CDN with edge caching. Both use global PoPs but serve different use cases.
questions.explanation: CloudFront: caches content at edges for HTTP/S — static/dynamic web content. Global Accelerator: no caching, routes ANY TCP/UDP traffic via AWS backbone to optimal endpoint — gaming, VoIP, APIs needing low latency without caching.

questions.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO in disaster recovery?
options: They are the same metric

RPO (Recovery Point Objective): maximum acceptable data loss — how old the oldest recoverable data can be. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): maximum acceptable downtime — how fast systems must be restored.
questions.explanation: DR strategies ranked by RTO/RPO: Backup/Restore (hours RTO/RPO, cheapest), Pilot Light (minutes, warm DB + minimal infra), Warm Standby (minutes, scaled-down full environment), Multi-Site Active/Active (near-zero, most expensive).

questions.question: What is Amazon ECS Task Definition?
options: An EC2 configuration template
A blueprint for an ECS task specifying: Docker image, CPU/memory, port mappings, environment variables, IAM role, logging configuration, and storage volumes — versioned and reusable.
questions.explanation: Task Definition = like a docker-compose file for ECS. Each revision is versioned. Task Role: IAM permissions for the container (access S3, DynamoDB). Execution Role: permissions for ECS agent to pull image and push logs.

questions.question: What is Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose vs Data Streams?
options: Data Streams is managed

Kinesis Data Streams: real-time, custom consumer code, millisecond latency, retain 1-365 days. Kinesis Firehose: fully managed delivery to S3/Redshift/Elasticsearch/Splunk, batch delivery (60s–15min buffer), no custom code.
questions.explanation: Use Data Streams when: need real-time (<1s), multiple consumers, long retention, custom processing. Use Firehose when: need simple ingestion to AWS destinations, no latency requirement, no consumer management.

questions.question: What is an EC2 Instance Profile?
options: A firewall rule set
A container for an IAM role that can be attached to an EC2 instance — allows applications on the instance to make AWS API calls with the role's permissions without hardcoding credentials.
questions.explanation: Instance Profile = the 'wrapper' for an IAM role when assigning to EC2. When code on EC2 calls AWS SDK, it automatically retrieves temporary credentials from EC2 Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254). Never hardcode keys in EC2.

questions.question: What is Amazon DynamoDB Streams?
options: A Kinesis stream replacement
Captures item-level changes (INSERT, MODIFY, DELETE) in a DynamoDB table as an ordered stream — enables event-driven architectures, cross-region replication, and audit trails via Lambda triggers.
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams: up to 24-hour retention, ordered by item. Stream records contain old/new images of changed items. Lambda can trigger on stream changes for: search indexing, real-time aggregations, cross-region replication (Global Tables).

questions.question: What is AWS CloudFormation StackSets?
options: A multi-stack CloudFormation feature
Extends CloudFormation to deploy stacks across multiple AWS accounts and regions with a single operation — enables centralized infrastructure governance across an AWS Organization.
questions.explanation: StackSets: deploy same template to multiple accounts/regions simultaneously. Self-managed: provide admin/execution role ARNs. Service-managed: integrates with AWS Organizations for automatic account inclusion. Used for: security baselines, guardrails, compliance enforcement.

questions.question: What is the difference between EC2 Dedicated Hosts and Dedicated Instances?
options: They are identical

Dedicated Hosts: specific physical server allocated to you — full visibility of sockets/cores, BYOL licensing, per-host billing. Dedicated Instances: run on dedicated hardware but AWS manages server allocation, per-instance billing.
questions.explanation: Dedicated Host: reserve specific physical server, use BYOL SQL Server/Windows licenses (per-socket pricing), compliance for regulations requiring physical isolation. Dedicated Instance: hardware not shared with other accounts but AWS manages placement.

questions.question: What is Amazon Inspector v2 vs Amazon Detective?
options: They are identical

Inspector: automated vulnerability scanning for EC2/ECR/Lambda — finds CVEs and network exposure. Detective: investigates security incidents by analyzing VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, GuardDuty findings using graph analytics.
questions.explanation: Inspector: preventive — scans for known CVEs in running workloads proactively. Detective: reactive — after a GuardDuty alert, Detective helps you understand the scope and timeline of the incident using historical data analysis.
